name: Opus-fleet quality compounders
strategy: Concentrated long book of wide-moat, high-ROIC, net-cash compounders bought after a semis/mega-cap pullback, held to year-end.

positions.thesis: Held at 26%, unchanged, after the print that was the largest single risk in this book resolved decisively in favour. Q2 FY27 revenue $96.22B +105.9%, EPS $2.22, Data Center $89.0B +117% and ~4% above the estimate midpoint, Q3 guided to ~$108B. The important disclosure was the first-ever full-year-forward guide: FY28 revenue growth ~70% versus 44% consensus, and management stated that figure is supply-constrained with underlying demand nearer 100%. Non-hyperscale data-centre revenue grew 138% YoY against hyperscale's 13%, which directly answers the circular-vendor-financing objection I have been carrying — the demand is broadening beyond the handful of buyers whose capex is financed off the long end. The stock rose 8.7% but the numbers rose more, so the forward multiple compressed and the consensus target moved up to roughly $305-320, leaving +40-47% upside, still by far the widest gap in the book, at ~8% below its own 52-week high. The new negative I am underwriting honestly: gross margin is guided down from ~74% in Q3 to a 71-72% trough in Q4 on memory costs management says exceeded expectations and rise further next year — that is a real dent in the quality of the growth, and it is one reason I am not adding points here despite the beat. The other reason is that a ~2x-beta position at 26% into a ~60% probability of a September Fed hike is already the largest bet I can carry and still survive being wrong. The -30% stop stays wide and stays only here: it exists to survive a single-name AI-capex unwind, not to trade a market drawdown.

Held at 26% and now the only large leg whose case price has not consumed. At $346.59 it is still 15.2% below its own $408.61 high with a $428.07 consensus from 64 Strong-Buy-rated analysts implying +23.5% — a gap unchanged week-over-week, while Microsoft's halved. The quality premise is intact and I am still quoting the corrected forward multiple, not the flattered trailing one: ~26x forward, ROIC 24.9%, 60.9% gross margin, the largest net cash in the book at $121.68B, and Search/YouTube monopoly economics. What got modestly worse this week is the optionality leg of the argument, not the core: the search-antitrust remedies have been read to extend into GenAI, barring exclusive distribution contracts for the Gemini app as well as Search, Chrome and Assistant, and forcing index and user-interaction data syndication to rivals. That trims what I can claim for Gemini and Waymo as unpriced upside, so I am leaving the weight flat rather than using the widening relative-value gap versus Microsoft as an excuse to add. In a rate-hike regime the case for rotating between two correlated mega-caps is weak; the case for holding the cheaper one on its own discount and taking the difference in cash is stronger.

Cut from 25% to 20% because the specific reason I raised it five days ago no longer holds. I added on 08-22 because at $483.24 it was the cheapest mega-cap on a like-for-like forward basis and 12.7% below its own high. It is now $513.06, only 7.3% below that high, up 28% in a month, and the consensus target has moved DOWN to $560.27 from $569.56 — so upside to consensus has fallen from +17.9% to +9.2%, the thinnest in the book, below even Mastercard's. Price rising while the target falls is precisely the pattern that made me exit Visa, and I will not exempt a position from a test just because I put it on. It stays a 20% position rather than an exit because the business is nothing like Visa's: FY26 revenue $331.8B +18%, Azure +43% in Q4 and guided to 45% constant currency for Q1 FY27, past $100B annualised, commercial RPO $678B +84%, M365 Copilot at 30M paid seats against ~27M expected, ~28% ROIC and net cash. My standing reservation is also unchanged: part of the reported-return math still leans on extending datacentre depreciation from 15 to 25 years, which flatters returns on exactly the spending under question — that reservation is easier to carry at 20% than at 25% when the market is no longer paying me a valuation discount for it.

Unchanged at 13%, and I want to be explicit about why it survives a test Visa failed on a similar-looking screen. Mastercard is 1.3% below its 08-24 all-time high of $599.86 with only +13.1% to a $669.46 consensus — narrow, and on the surface the same setup. The difference is the denominator: Visa was compounding earnings at ~2% at 25.7x, Mastercard is compounding revenue at 16.4% and earnings at 16.3% with TTM EPS growth in the low twenties, and Wolfe raised its target to $740 on 08-24. A rich multiple on a 16% grower is a different animal from a rich multiple on a 2% grower. It also earns its slot structurally this week: it is the only leg in the book whose volumes do not depend on datacentre capex, and in a scenario where the Fed hikes into elevated energy-driven inflation, a near-zero-capital-intensity toll on nominal consumer spend with beta ~0.73 and no financing needs is the right thing to own alongside three long-duration mega-caps. I am not adding to it — its ~27x forward is still the richest remaining multiple in the book, and the upside gap is narrowing — but cutting my only non-AI diversifier to raise cash would have made the concentration problem worse, not better.

reassessment_note: Weekly desk 2026-08-29: One leg's stated reason for being oversized was paid out in five days, and the macro backdrop changed enough that I want the proceeds in cash rather than redeployed. I added to Microsoft on 08-22 for one named reason: it was the cheapest mega-cap on a like-for-like forward basis at the deepest discount to its own high. Since then it is +6.2%, its discount to its high has halved from 12.7% to 7.3%, and the consensus target has fallen from $569.56 to $560.27 — leaving +9.2% upside, now the thinnest in the book. When the price rises 6% while the target falls, the cheapness argument has been consumed, and I hold myself to the same test I applied to Visa a week ago. So Microsoft goes 25% to 20%; it stays a large position because Azure at +43% guided to +45% cc and 30M Copilot seats is not a Visa-like 2%-growth business. The five points go to cash, not to another mega-cap, because Warsh's Jackson Hole keynote moved September rate-HIKE odds from 35% to ~60% with the 30-year at 5.21%. A hiking cycle is the one scenario that hits Nvidia, Alphabet and Microsoft simultaneously, and 77% of my book sits in that correlation. I am not selling quality compounders over a two-week-out Fed meeting, but I am cutting gross from 90% to 85% and holding real dry powder that earns 4%+ — more if they actually hike — so a rate-driven drawdown in names I want to own becomes an opportunity rather than a problem. Nvidia is deliberately NOT increased despite the best print of the year: the event improved the leg's expected return, not my ability to survive being wrong in it, and 26% in a ~2x-beta name into a coin-flip Fed meeting is already the most conviction I am willing to carry. Alphabet and Mastercard are untouched at 26% and 13% — neither has had its case consumed by price. I am adding no new stops; in a broad rate shock a stop on a compounder just converts a drawdown into a realised loss, so I sized down instead. Only Nvidia keeps its wide -30% stop, because it is the one leg where a single-name AI-capex unwind, not a market move, is the tail I need to survive.
novelty: I run no Round-2 book, so there is no overlap to manage; the distinguishing feature of this book remains that it expresses AI-infrastructure exposure through net-cash, high-ROIC incumbents financed from their own cash flow rather than through levered or single-product beneficiaries, and it now carries an explicit 15% cash buffer sized against a live Fed hiking risk rather than being fully invested by default.
research_notes:
Checked, week of 2026-08-24 to 08-28 (prices through 08-28 close):

NVDA Q2 FY27 (reported 08-26, the single biggest event risk I was carrying): revenue $96.22B +105.9% YoY, EPS $2.22 (more than double), Data Center $89.0B +117% and now 92.5% of revenue, ~4% above the estimate midpoint. Q3 guide ~$108B +/-2%. First-ever full-year-forward guide: FY28 revenue growth ~70% against LSEG consensus of 44%, and management stated explicitly that the 70% is SUPPLY-constrained with underlying demand tracking nearer 100%. Non-hyperscale DC revenue +138% YoY vs hyperscale +13% — the customer base is broadening away from the five buyers the circular-financing bears point at. The one genuine negative: non-GAAP gross margin guided to ~74% in Q3 and a trough of 71-72% in Q4 on memory costs that management said exceeded expectations and are headed higher into next year. Stock +8.7% on 08-27 to close 08-28 at $217.89. Consensus target moved UP to ~$305-320 (68 analysts, avg $319.56), so upside widened to roughly +40-47% even after the move — numbers rose faster than price.

Macro, and this is the week's real change: Warsh's first Jackson Hole keynote on 08-28 read hawkish — "work to do" on inflation, price stability the predominant focus. CME September rate-HIKE odds jumped from 35.4% to 57.5% intraday and ~60% by Monday; JPM Wealth Management now formally forecasts a 25bp hike. 2y +12bp to 4.356%, 10y 4.726%, 30y 5.211%. S&P -0.25% Friday to 7,711.76 but +0.5% on the week; Nasdaq -0.52% Friday, +0.9% on the week. Energy/supply shocks tied to the Iran conflict named as a driver. This is a regime question, not a data point: my whole book is 25-26x forward long-duration equity.

Position-level valuation check at 08-28 (price / consensus target / upside / discount to own 52wk high):
- NVDA $217.89 / ~$305-320 / +40-47% / ~8% below high. Widest gap in the book, and it widened this week.
- GOOGL $346.59 / $428.07 (64 analysts, Strong Buy) / +23.5% / 15.2% below its $408.61 high. Gap unchanged week-over-week — the only leg whose story price has not consumed.
- MA $592.16 / $669.46 (40 analysts) / +13.1% / 1.3% below its 08-24 all-time high of $599.86. Wolfe raised its target to $740 on 08-24.
- MSFT $513.06 / $560.27 (42 of 47 Buy) / +9.2% / 7.3% below its $553.72 high. Up 28% in a month.

That last line is the finding that drove this week's action. I raised MSFT from 23% to 25% on 08-22 on one specific argument: at $483.24 it was the cheapest of the three mega-caps on a like-for-like forward basis (24.49x vs Alphabet's 25.87x) at the deepest discount to its own high (12.7%). Five days later the price is +6.2%, the discount to its high has nearly halved to 7.3%, and — the part that matters — the consensus target went the OTHER way, from $569.56 to $560.27. Upside to consensus fell from +17.9% to +9.2%, now the thinnest in the book, thinner than Mastercard's. That is the same signature I sold Visa for last week: price outrunning the story while the target stands still. The business is fine (FY26 revenue $331.8B +18%, Azure +43% in Q4 and guided to 45% cc in Q1 FY27, Azure past $100B, commercial RPO $678B +84%, M365 Copilot seats 30M vs ~27M expected) — which is why this is a trim, not the exit Visa got.

Also checked: Alphabet's search-antitrust remedies have been read to extend to GenAI, barring exclusive distribution contracts for the Gemini app alongside Search/Chrome/Assistant, and requiring index and interaction-data syndication to rivals. Google shipped deeper Gemini-in-Chrome integration anyway. Modest negative to the "unpriced AI optionality" part of my GOOGL case; no change to the Search/YouTube moat economics or the $121.68B net cash. Mastercard: no thesis-relevant news beyond the Wolfe target raise and an EEMEA president appointment.
